title: Hybrid fast-path handshake: low-latency streaming + safe tool-call UX (PRD sketch)
content:
Purpose and summary:
This sketch proposes a low-latency "hybrid fast-path" for the Hosted API that lets callers start receiving partial, token-level streaming output immediately while simultaneously negotiating a safe, resumable tool-call handshake and a soft-typed structured-output contract. The goal is to: (1) minimize time-to-first-byte for interactive experiences, (2) enable reliable tool invocations without blocking the UI, and (3) provide ergonomic SDK primitives that make progressive results easy to consume and validate on the client.

Problem statement:
- Modern clients (chat UI, coding assistants, search assistants) need near-instant partial text to show typing latency < 100ms perceived.
- At the same time they want structured tool-calls (e.g., run_search, run_lambda, open_url) that must be validated server-side for safety and consistency.
- Current patterns force a tradeoff: either wait until model decides to call a tool (blocking until the model finishes) or stream raw tokens and try to retroactively detect/repair tool calls on the client. Both lead to poor UX or fragile client logic.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Time-to-first-token median < 50ms on common routes (us-east-hosted) for small prompt sizes.
- End-to-end tool-call initiation latency (from first tool intent token to validated tool execution trigger) < 300ms in the fast-path.
- Clients can render partial text immediately and progressively apply an authoritative structured output once handshake completes.
- SDK provides a simple reactive API: onPartial(token), onActionProposal(actionCandidate), onActionConfirmed(actionRecord), onSessionResume().

Non-goals:
- This sketch does not replace existing full synchronous tool-call API or guarantee identical output semantics for every legacy client.
- It does not require every existing model to be rewritten; compatibility layers will be provided.

Design overview (high level):
- Serve two related streams for a single logical request: the "fast stream" (unreliable partial tokens + minimal annotations) and the "control channel" (handshake messages, action proposals, schema diffs, final authoritative frame). Both are delivered over the same HTTP/2 or WebSocket connection and multiplexed with lightweight framing.
- Fast stream: delivers incremental tokens ASAP with minimal metadata (seq, token_type, approximate_token_offsets). Fast stream always emits, even if the model later chooses a different action.
- Control channel: emits structured messages (action.proposal, action.validation, action.confirmation, schema.patch) that are canonical. When control channel confirms an action, the SDK should mark the authoritative state and optionally patch previously rendered tokens (patch diff provided).
- Handshake: client includes a session-handshake header with token_budget, preferred_schema, and trust_level. Server responds with a handshake_ack indicating supported fast-path semantics and whether action execution is allowed for this session (based on policy, account tier, and model confidence).

Example message flow (simplified):
1) Client POST /v1/streams with headers: X-RI-Session: {"session_id", token_budget, preferred_schema}
2) Server responds 200 and upgrades to streaming frames. Fast stream begins emitting tokens ("fast: 'Scheduling a meeting' ...").
3) At token N, model emits an action intent token (tool-call intent). Fast stream includes a lightweight annotation {action_hint: "schedule_event"} alongside tokens.
4) Control channel emits action.proposal: {id, name: "schedule_event", args_snippet, confidence}
5) SDK surfaces a UI affordance (suggested action) but does not run it yet. Client may accept/modify or wait for confirmation.
6) Server does local validation (policy, schema) and emits action.confirmation when safe: {id, status: "confirmed", execution_id}.
7) If confirmed, server may emit a patch frame to update previously streamed tokens to the authoritative structured result (for example replace a partial natural language description with the structured event JSON and a short human-readable summary).

Structured output and soft schemas:
- Introduce soft schemas: lightweight, client-provided JSON schemas that can be used for early validation but are not strictly enforced at generation time.
- Control channel will stream schema.patch messages that indicate required/optional fields and soft-type hints ("datetime: ISO-8601", "email: needs-local-lookup").
- On confirmation, server returns an authoritative structured payload that should be treated as source-of-truth for downstream tooling. SDK will include helpers to coerce/validate the final payload against the last known schema.patch.

SDK ergonomics (patterns we want):
- Minimal surface: one top-level StreamSession object per logical request.
- Event callbacks / async iterators: onPartial(token), onTokenMetadata(meta), onActionProposal(proposal), onActionConfirmed(action), onPatch(patch), onError(err), close().
- Declarative bindings: session.bindAction('schedule_event', {confirm: true|false, uiHints}) to let SDK decide whether to auto-confirm low-risk actions.
- Local optimistic rendering: SDK offers a small patch-queue to show optimistic changes (e.g., fill form fields) that are visually distinct until action.confirmation arrives.
- Backpressure and cancelation: session.requestMoreTokens(n) and session.cancelReason(reason). Default policy is server-driven, but client can request lower throughput to limit token bursts for mobile.

API sketches (payload examples):
- POST /v1/streams
  headers: X-RI-Session: {"session_id":"s_abc","token_budget":512,"preferred_schema":"event_v2"}
  body: {"model":"rwd-chat-2","input":"Plan a team sync next week"}
- Example fast-frame (binary/frame-level): {"seq":128, "t":"token", "text":"Schedul","meta": {"approx_offset":0}}
- Example control message: {"type":"action.proposal","id":"p_42","name":"schedule_event","args_snippet":"Next Tuesday at 3pm","confidence":0.72}
- Example confirmation: {"type":"action.confirmation","id":"p_42","status":"confirmed","execution_id":"exec_9001","payload":{"start":"2025-03-03T15:00:00Z","attendees":["alice@acme.com"]}}

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- Emit token.latency histogram (time from request accepted -> first token; and per-token intervals).
- action.proposal.latency, action.confirmation.latency, schema.patch.latency.
- track reconciliation.events: count of optimistic patches that were later reverted vs accepted.
- Add route-level flags for fast-path eligibility and fast-path fallbacks (e.g., fallback.reason = 'policy_block' or 'model_incompat').
- SDK should emit client-side metrics: render_lag_ms, optimistic_patches, reconcilations_count. These metrics must map to Redwood Console dashboards and be attached to request ids for debugging.

Compatibility and migration:
- Backwards compatible: clients that do not support the control channel still get the fast stream (tokens) and can continue to use heuristic tool detection, but we will mark them as missing handshake and gradually deprecate heuristics after adoption thresholds.
- Migration plan: start by enabling fast-path on a small subset of traffic for internal customers and early partners. Provide an emulation shim in older SDK versions to translate control messages into existing callbacks.

Security and policy notes:
- Control channel must be authoritative for action execution decisions. Fast stream annotations are advisory only and must never trigger side effects.
- Handshake response includes an executable_actions boolean derived from policy engine + account settings + runtime confidence. If executable_actions=false, server will refuse confirmations and instead publish a reason.
- Authentication/authorization unchanged: every action.confirmation includes an execution_id bound to the request and the user context; actions must be recorded in audit logs and surfaced in the Console.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (internal): internal-only flag, instrument telemetry, validate patch reconciliation UX with internal apps (2 weeks).
- Phase 1 (partners): enable for 5 partner integrations, collect metrics, iterate SDK ergonomics (4 weeks).
- Phase 2 (beta): opt-in for all customers on hosted-api with feature flag; provide migration docs and SDK vX with default off (8 weeks).
- Phase 3 (GA): enable fast-path for eligible routes by default; monitor regressions and open emergency rollback toggle.

Operational concerns and failure modes:
- Reconciliation churn: frequent patch reverts can lead to confusing UX. We will implement heuristics to limit optimistic patching under high churn (e.g., stop optimistic patches after N reverts).
- Control channel latency spikes: if control messages are delayed, clients should continue to render tokens and surface a non-blocking UI for action confirmation.
- Partial schema drift: provide schema-versioned patches so SDK can gracefully handle missing fields.

Open questions (for follow-up):
- Should we allow client-driven auto-confirmation for low-risk actions by default for certain account tiers?
- How strongly should SDK attempt to patch previously streamed tokens vs inserting an explicit authoritative block? (UX and accessibility concerns)
- What is the canonical wire format for frames? JSON over WS is easiest for adoption; binary framing (e.g., proto) will reduce size but increase adoption friction.
- How will deduplication work when clients reconnect mid-session? Do we assign monotonic frame cursors?

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: prototype multiplexed frames over HTTP/2 streaming and a minimal control channel (ENG: Diego Morales, 2w).
- SDK: implement StreamSession prototype with callback-based and async-iterator API (DX: Asha Patel, 2w).
- Product: write partner-facing beta guide and migration checklist (Product: Riley Chen, 1w).
- SRE/Telemetry: add token.latency, action.confirmation.latency, reconciliation.rate to Console (SRE: Liara Novak, 1w).

Appendix: UX micro-pattern examples (client-side):
- "Soft insert" — show authoritative structured action as a visually boxed element inline; keep original text as collapsed transcript.
- "Undo affordance" — allow user to undo an auto-confirmed low-risk action for 10s after confirmation.
- "Confirmation snackbar" — non-blocking confirmation UI when action.confirmation arrives (supports quick edit).

Notes and references:
- Related internal PRDs: CONFLUENCE-022 (progressive schemas), CONFLUENCE-089 (streaming SDK ergonomics).
- Prototype artifacts: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-prototypes/stream-session (early code).

This is a working sketch; feedback on the control-channel message shapes, SDK surface, and policy interactions is requested.
